items.title: Keeping Small CLI Text Utilities Fast and Type-Safe in Crystal
items.author: shardcraft34
items.content:
Hello everyone, I have been writing a few small CLI text-processing utilities in Crystal lately, and wanted to share a couple of habits that kept compile times fast and code easy to follow.

Coming from interpreted scripting languages, having Ruby-like syntax with static type checks caught several subtle nil-handling bugs right at compile time. Keeping union types small and explicit at module boundaries—and using for quick unit tests on each parser helper—made refactoring painless. Looking forward to learning more idioms from the community here.

items.title: Proposal: Add support for packed properties
items.author: Jochen
items.content:
I recently explored some memory optimizations in the compiler, and one of them was packing booleans and enums into an UInt32, saving quite some space.

If the etc. macros were to support this, other applications could also benefit. I propose extending these macros to support the following named parameters:

  • property flag : Bool = false, packed: @field packs the variable in the minimum number of required bits in instance variable
  • Nilable fields get an extra bit as nil marker, or a parameter that designates one value as the nil marker
  • Packing booleans: e.g. 8 booleans from 8 bytes → 1 byte
  • Packing for nilable integers/small enums: e.g. 2 UInt16? from 32 bytes → 4 bytes

The macro can automatically allocate the required bits in the field, check if the required amount of bits is exceeded, or if there are any collisions.

We could also of course create a separate macro for this, but using looks nicer imo.

items.title: Crystal compiler memory experiments (- 13-18% total, - 30-40% heap) for fun…
items.author: Jochen
items.content:
…and maybe profit. Had some time to play around with the compiler and tried to reduce memory consumption.

Some results for three test subjects (compiler itself, Lucky, and one own app), measured on a 2021 MacBook Pro against d8d99aa

The patches are available here, and are and . Some also (for now) break the Compiler API in small ways (e.g. returning instead of ). No work put in to make them nice. Compiler newbie here, and I am also not sure if every one of them should really be applied… I would be very grateful im someone could have a look if these patches make sense and the results are reproducible.

Also, up to here it was fun. However, my motivation to put more work into something that will not get merged is somewhat limited, so please feel free to give an indication which ones make sense to you, and I will polish them and submit a PR for those.

Report memory use and each garbage collection in and prints the heap in use, the heap size and the process memory; adds a line per collection. Measurement only, no change to the compiler’s behavior.
Store nilable value fields of AST nodes without a unionStores always-positive fields as an with for : 4 bytes instead of a 16-byte union.
Store small properties of AST nodes in bit fieldsAdds , which packs s into 1 bit and enums into as few bits as they need in one field.
Store more properties of AST nodes in bit fieldsMoves the flags of and other nodes into the bit field and widens to 32 bits.
Store the special variables a def assigns as bit fieldsReplaces the of with two flags for and . and get 16 bytes smaller.
Store the definition a def overrides without its metadata stores the overridden instead of a 32-byte and builds the metadata on request.
Store rarely used fields of in an extension objectMoves fields that few calls use into , allocated on first use. gets 64 bytes smaller.
Store rarely used fields of in an extension objectDoes the same for with ; moves to . gets 96 bytes smaller.
Keep dependencies and observers in two shared slotsExtend on the existing optimization by sharing link slots between dependencies and observers, to allocate less arrays.
Replace with a node that holds the variable holds the variable itself, so an with an unreachable branch no longer allocates a filter object per variable.
Store a single target def in the call without an arrayA call stores its only target def directly and keeps an array only for several.
Store a single name and one target in A with one name stores the string itself and keeps an array only for several names.
Store the enclosing call in a third link slotThe rarely set enclosing call moves into a third slot shared with dependencies and observers, replacing a field of every node.
Move the type binding state of nodes into Adds above with everything except the location, so the nodes the type inference creates for itself go without one.
Release the type bindings before codegenClears all type bindings after the semantic phase, so codegen runs with that memory freed (with option to disable).
Release the visitors that calls, blocks and constants keepThe release pass also drops the of each call and constant, and the binder and variables of each block (with option to disable).

items.title: CRShader - Crystal as a shading language (for godot and beyond)
items.author: sol.vin
items.content:
Hey everyone! I’ve been building , a shader transpiler and live-coding toolchain written in Crystal (powered by Lapis) for , as well as standalone targets such as glsl.

It lets you write GPU shaders in a type-safe, idiomatic Crystal DSL that compiles to , , and at .

  • Define , , and types with predicates and mutating methods—lowered to structs + functions with dead-code tree-shaking.
  • Left-to-right UV warps, sampling, grading & blend modes (UV.tile(2.0).wave(8.0, 0.02)).
  • & auto-pack / buffers and push constants.
  • adds live viewport heatmaps & / checks, stripped to with .
  • Live Godot & Standalone Apps: Direct loading & dock in Godot, CLI/node codegen, plus standalone apps.
shader_type :spatial

class FresnelRim
  color : Vec3
  power : Float32

  def boost!(k : Float32) : Void
    @power *= k # `!` -> `inout FresnelRim _self`
  end

  def evaluate(n : Vec3, v : Vec3) : Vec3
    @color * ((1.0 - dot(n, v).saturate) ** @power)
  end
end

uniform rim_boost : Float32 = 1.2

def fragment
  rim = FresnelRim.new(vec3(0.35, 0.8, 1.0), 2.5)
  rim.boost!(rim_boost)
  EMISSION = rim.evaluate(NORMAL, VIEW)
end

items.title: System View – another GTK4 desktop app written in Crystal
items.author: magynhard
items.content:
With Black Friday coming up, I was talking to my brother about our PC hardware and possible upgrades. I just wanted a quick overview of what I’ve actually got – motherboard, CPU, socket, GPU, RAM, and so on.

Much like with Disk View, I couldn’t really find a modern Linux tool that gave me the simple, clean overview I was looking for (and get used by Windows in the past). Tools like HardInfo offer plenty of details, but sometimes I just want the essentials at a glance.

System View shows your hardware, connected devices, and some live system information in a clean, native GTK4 interface, with more details available when needed.

Some sections also include shortcuts to the corresponding GNOME Settings pages, so you can jump straight from viewing your hardware information to configuring it. Drives have a shortcut to DiskView if installed, of course.

I used Disk View as a blueprint, including the GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds AppImage and Flatpak packages for each release.

While working on it, I also expanded Disk View with quite a few additional translations, and System View now supports multiple languages as well.

Once again, Crystal has proven to be a great fit for native GTK4 development. I think it’ll remain my go-to language for GTK4 desktop apps for the foreseeable future.

Coming from Ruby, where I struggled quite a bit with creating desktop releases that were easy to distribute, integrate and maintain, Crystal feels like a much better fit. Its compiled nature and tooling provide a solid foundation for desktop applications. I actually think GTK4 could be a great opportunity for Crystal to gain more traction. The combination feels really natural to me, and I’d love to see more desktop apps built this way.

Like Disk View, the project was AI-agent-engineered.

Nothing groundbreaking, just another little tool I wanted to have. Maybe someone else will find it useful too!

Feedback is always welcome!

items.title: Compiler memory usage/GC
items.author: Jochen
items.content:
While looking at the compiler, I noticed that has a boolean flag in the middle of its properties, that costs 8 bytes because of padding. Moving to the beginning would fit it into the padding after the type ID.

However, testing that with compiling the compiler lead to a smaller heap, and the GC doing more collections, thus adding runtime. Which lead me to look a bit into the GC. It may be that there are some phases where GC takes up time and is not very effective (not freeing a lot). Maybe fiddling with the initial heap size, and turning off GC in some phases would speed things up a bit?

Question is, is that something I put time into? Any interest in PRs in this area?

items.title: LLVM 23 reduces release compilation time by nearly 12% compared with LLVM 22
items.author: zw963
items.content:
I noticed a substantial compilation-time difference between LLVM 22 and 23 while cross-compiling my Lucky application, crystal_china.

Both compilers were , running natively in AMD64 Podman containers and generating ARM64 musl release object files. The machine was an AMD Ryzen 7 7840HS running Arch Linux.

LLVM code generation ()
Official Crystal Alpine image, LLVM 22.1.3

Compilation was 20.46s faster, an 11.7% reduction. LLVM code generation alone was 12.8% faster and accounted for essentially the entire improvement.

The source, target and release flags were the same. Dependency installation, asset preparation, container startup and linking were excluded.

The script and benchmarks were produced using Codex 6.1 Sol High.

On an AMD64 Linux machine with rootless Podman:

git clone https://github.com/crystal-china/website.git crystal_china
cd crystal_china
git checkout 1fe7ca5
bash script/benchmark_llvm.sh

The single-file script prepares dependencies and frontend assets. Before timing each compiler, it runs:

crystal build "${args[@]}" --no-codegen

This compiles and caches the helper programs used by macros, without generating the application’s file. The script then times a full application compilation, generating a new file without reusing previous application object files.

Both compilers run sequentially. ARM64 files and logs are saved under bin/llvm-benchmark/{22,23}. There is no linking step.

The script checks for Crystal 1.22.3 and the expected LLVM major versions. Alpine edge is rolling, so its package versions may change.

This is not a strictly LLVM-only experiment: the distribution environments and compiler builds also differ. However, the improvement is concentrated almost entirely in the LLVM phase. Has anyone observed a similar improvement with LLVM 23?

items.title: Deploying a Kemal app on a Canadian VPS
items.author: 4GoodHosting
items.content:
I’m getting ready to deploy a small Kemal app for a client in Canada, and it will store some customer details. PIPEDA covers most private businesses here, and BC public bodies and Quebec’s Law 25 add stricter rules about where personal information is stored, so the server and database will both stay in a Canadian data centre. This is my plan so far:

  1. pin the Crystal version in CI and on the server, and commit shard.lock.
  2. on CI for the same target as the server.
  3. use the official Alpine image with so the VPS needs no extra libraries.
  4. a systemd unit with restart on failure, running as a non-root user.
  5. Nginx or Caddy in front for TLS, with Kemal listening only on localhost.
  6. Postgres through crystal-pg, with migrations run before the new binary starts.
  7. nightly database dumps copied to storage that also stays in Canada.

For those running Crystal in production: have you moved to multi-threaded builds yet, and how do you handle zero-downtime restarts?

items.title: So how are people actually using this LLM thing?
items.author: Xen
items.content:
To counter the threads about the merits of LLM coding a bit, and make it a bit more practical and, hopefully, inspirational, how about a thread about people using it, and what they’re using? All levels of usage welcome, from “I just paste questions to ChatGPT” to “I got a server burning tokens 24/7 with a multi-agent, multi-model, custom written harness”.

For some reason I started out with OpenCode and Gemini. The latter because I could pull a API token from work. But being an old geezer that tries to avoid having to learn new thing unless hard pressed, I quickly pivoted to running OC as an APC server and using for Emacs as the frontend.

But when OC did the cardinal sin of messing with my workflow (they changed how plan mode worked), I started shopping around. Tried Hermes, but it’s a beast, and I wasn’t sure what the hell it was doing, so I moved on to Pi for a little while.

Lately I’ve been pressured into using Claude Code, which people at work tells me is the best thing since sliced bread.

Being the suspicious old sysadmin type that I am, I’ve locked it down inside a container without access to any of my files, which somewhat limits its magic. A like-minded coworker has produced an MCP server that gives it read-only and sanitized access to our core services (Github, Jira, chat, timetracking and Drive). And as most of our projects utilizes containers, which is difficult to work with from inside one, I ended up getting Claude to code an MCP server it could use to ask to run something outside the container, which pops up a nice prompt in Emacs for approval.

So in usage I just open a session in a project and ask it questions and tells it what to do. Then I review what it did (loosely if it’s just a personal tool, more rigorously when work), before committing.

I don’t let it commit, write commit messages, PR descriptions or anything else meant for human consumption.

Not using any skills, though I’m considering installing Ponytail again.

I’m not to happy about being bound up on Anthropic, but it’s what work has decided to pay for, apart from what we get with our Google subscription. I must admit that Claude seems just a tad more smart than Gemini, but I wonder how much is the model, and how much is the harness. Considering spinning up Pi with Gemini for some comparisons.

items.title: CrystKit – desktop apps in Crystal with a web frontend
items.author: naqvis
items.content:
I’ve been working on CrystKit for years, and it’s finally ready to show. It’s a desktop application framework for Crystal: backend in Crystal, UI in HTML/CSS/JS, running in a native window on the system WebView (WebKit on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows). No bundled Chromium, no Node at runtime, one binary.

app = CrystKit::App.new
app.plugin CrystKit::Plugins::Dialog.new

app.async "notes.count", String, timeout: 1.minute do |dir, _|
  Dir.glob("#{dir}/**/*.md").size
end

app.window(title: "Notes", html: File.read("frontend/index.html"))
app.run

const ipc = window.__CRYSTKIT_IPC__;
const dir = await ipc.invoke("dialog.select_folder", { title: "Notes" });
const count = await ipc.invoke("notes.count", dir);

That’s the whole model: plugins expose native features as commands, you add your own, the frontend calls both through one bridge. Everything else builds on it.

  • Command signatures define the payload; bad input never reaches your handler. commands run off the UI thread with a timeout.
  • Capability-based security. Native access needs an explicit capability (, , …) and a resource scope (paths, URLs, commands), declared in a manifest. Per-window grants, temporary grants, and events the frontend can’t spoof.
  • Reactive state and streaming. Backend-owned state slices push JSON Patch diffs to the frontend; channels stream progress, process output, log tails.
  • : filesystem, file watching, SQLite, OS keychain, HTTP/WebSocket, processes and shell, dialogs, clipboard, tray, menus, global shortcuts, notifications, window effects, auto-updater, single instance, deep links, hardware, power/idle/theme monitors, speech, biometrics, printing. Your own plugins use the same interface and security model.
  • crystkit init / dev / build / bundle – live reload in development, then , //, / or a portable build.

Tested on macOS, Linux and Windows; the spec suite runs headless on all three.

items.title: [ANN] odf v0.1.0: Pure-Crystal OASIS ODF 1.3 .ods reader and writer, zero dependencies
items.author: renich
items.content:
I just tagged , a pure-Crystal OASIS OpenDocument Format 1.3 shard built strictly on Crystal’s standard library (, , ) with zero runtime dependencies and zero C wrappers.

I needed self-contained static binaries that could generate and parse real spreadsheets with live formulas and proper styling without shelling out to Python or LibreOffice, so I built from the ground up.

  • Writer (Odf::Spreadsheet::Workbook): Multi-sheet workbooks, typed cells (, , , , , , , ), live OpenFormula expressions, cell merges, frozen panes, autofilters, and reusable styles/number formats.
  • Hardened Reader (): XXE-safe XML parsing, streaming Zip-bomb byte quotas, and bounded repeat-cell expansion.
  • Extensible Core (): and are document-agnostic, so adding , , and support does not require touching the container engine.
require "odf"

workbook = Odf::Spreadsheet::Workbook.new do |book|
  book.currency_style("usd", symbol: "$", decimals: 2, negative_red: true)

  book.sheet("BOM") do |sheet|
    sheet.freeze(rows: 1)
    sheet.header_row(["Qty", "Item", "Unit Price", "Total"])

    sheet.row do |row|
      row.integer(4)
      row.text("NVMe OSD Node")
      row.currency(12_500.00, style: "usd")
      row.formula("=[.A2]*[.C2]", cached: 50_000.00, style: "usd")
    end
  end
end

workbook.save("bom.ods")

doc = Odf::Spreadsheet::Reader.open("bom.ods")
puts doc.sheet("BOM")[1][3].as_f # => 50000.0

If anyone is interested in tackling , , or modules on top of , contributions and feedback are very welcome!

items.title: Disk View – a very small GTK4 desktop app and project blueprint
items.author: magynhard
items.content:
I’d like to share a little side project I’ve been working on: Disk View.

It’s a pretty simple Linux desktop app that shows all your drives, partitions, and their disk usage in one compact overview.

I wasn’t really happy with GNOME’s default Disks app when all I wanted was a quick overview of how much space was used across my drives. So I ended up building my own little tool. Nothing particularly fancy, but it does exactly what I was looking for.

The app is written in Crystal using GTK4 and libadwaita.

What might actually be more interesting to the Crystal community than the app itself is the project setup. It could serve as a starting point or reference for anyone interested in building native GTK4 desktop applications with Crystal. Especially the GitHub workflow and setup for AppImage and Flatpak.

  • GTK4/libadwaita integration using Crystal bindings

  • A fairly typical GNOME desktop app structure

  • Translations for multiple languages

  • A GitHub Actions workflow that automatically builds AppImage and Flatpak packages and attaches them to GitHub releases

The project was AI-agent-engineered and took only a few days, as i already had ported another experimental project, that i originally wrote with Ruby and GTK4. But after it was running well, it did not do well on other systems … this was one of my main reasons to finally spend more time and interest on Crystal. But the original problem that brought me to Crystal was another NodeJS (CLI) project, that i will port soon to crystal, after i have released a stable release of my Crystal Language Plugin for Jetbrains IDEs.

A big thanks to Hugo Parente Lima (@hugopl) for his work on the GTK4 bindings and GI-Crystal. Without projects like these, building native GTK applications in Crystal would be a lot harder. Really appreciate the effort!

Anyway, I thought I’d share it here in case someone finds either the app or parts of its implementation useful.

Feedback is always welcome!
